stories.headline: News In Frames: Velvety crimson is Kashmir’s treasure
stories.deck: Deeply rooted in Kashmir’s culinary heritage, the cockscomb flower lends a rich red hue to traditional cuisine; the petals, which are sun-dried and preserved for year-round use, serve as an indispensable ingredient in wazwan
stories.bodyText:
The cockscomb flower (Celosia cristata) is recognisable by its distinctive, velvety, fan-shaped crest that resembles a rooster’s comb. Rich crimson pigment is concentrated in the dense and highly textured folds of the blossom and these petals are harvested and dried to give traditional Kashmiri dishes their signature ruby-red colour.
Cultivated in the fertile valleys of Kashmir, these blossoms are carefully handpicked at peak bloom, sun-dried to preserve their intense natural pigments, and stored for year-round culinary use. The dried flowers are locally known as mawal.
Mawal holds a sacred status in the wazwan — the famous multi-course royal feast prepared by master chefs known as wazas. It imparts a subtle, earthy undertone that seamlessly complements heavy spices without overpowering them. Mawal is usually sold in the traditional markets of Srinagar. To release the signature crimson colour, the dried flower petals or mawal powder is steeped in hot water. The resulting rich, ruby extract is then strained directly into simmering gravies.
Mawal is indispensable in classics like rogan josh (meat curry), adding colour and flavour to the famed gravy alongside mild Kashmiri red chillies. It is also added to dishes like rista (spiced meatball curry), mirchi korma (chillies curry), and vegetarian specialities like dum aloo (potato curry).
Mawal reflects Kashmir’s deep-rooted heritage of using local flora for natural, organic cooking. In traditional medicine, it is valued for its soothing and cooling properties, making rich, meat-heavy wazwan courses easier to digest.
As an irreplaceable element of Kashmir’s gastronomic identity, mawal helps elevate every feast into a visually stunning and authentic experience.

stories.headline: 'Not good news': Ex-India star questions India's handling of Vaibhav Sooryavanshi
stories.deck: Mohammad Kaif has expressed concerns regarding India's choice to omit Vaibhav Sooryavanshi from the fourth T20I match. Sooryavanshi participated in the second and third T20Is, replacing the injured Ishan Kishan. Kaif believes that consistent opportunities would aid in boosting Sooryavanshi's confidence as a budding player. India leads the series 3-1 but suffered a substantial defeat in the fourth…
stories.bodyText:
Former India batter 
Mohammad Kaif
 has questioned India's decision to leave Vaibhav Sooryavanshi out of the fourth T20I against New Zealand. He believes the young batter should have been given another opportunity, especially after India had already secured the series.
Sooryavanshi played the second and third T20Is after 
Ishan Kishan
 was ruled out due to injury. However, when Kishan returned to the team, the youngster had to make way for him in the fourth match, which India lost.
Kaif feels that giving Sooryavanshi a consistent run would have helped build his confidence. He also pointed out that India had already taken an unassailable 3-0 lead before the fourth match.
"Not good news for Sooryavanshi"
Kaif believes that leaving out a young player after giving him just two opportunities is not the right approach.
"This is not good news for the player (not getting a consistent run). He is a potential superstar. And you have seen what he can do. In the third T20I, he and Abhishek Sharma scored 100 runs in six overs. For his confidence-building, it is not good news for any player, even if he is a veteran," Kaif said on his YouTube channel.
He felt the fourth T20I was the right opportunity to give Sooryavanshi another game, as India had already won the series.
"There was an opportunity to play him in this game. You had already won the series. You need to see the situation you are in during the series. On one side, you left Bhuvneshwar out and said you would bring in new players. Vaibhav is also new, so why not give him the same treatment? You are grooming Mayank Yadav and Prince Yadav. By the same logic, he should have played. The platform was well set."
Will Sooryavanshi get another chance in the fifth T20I?
India will look to make a few changes when they face New Zealand in the fifth and final T20I at Seddon Park on Sunday.
India lead the series 3-1 but suffered a heavy 87-run defeat in Auckland in the fourth match. The result could prompt the team management to make changes to its playing XI.
Sooryavanshi is among the players who could return to the side. 
Sanju Samson
 could make way for the youngster after struggling for runs in the series.
Samson scored 67 in the opening T20I in Christchurch but has managed just 14, 18 and four in his next three innings.
The final match could give Sooryavanshi another opportunity to impress as India look to finish the series with a victory.
Kaif questions Kishan's return to the playing XI
Kaif also felt that India could have rested Ishan Kishan instead of bringing him straight back into the playing XI.
Kishan returned after recovering from an injury and took over wicketkeeping duties. According to Kaif, if the batter was not fully fit, there was no need to rush him back, especially with the series already decided.
"Ishan came back from injury and was keeping wickets. My gut feeling is that he did not want to run much. Maybe that's why he was given the gloves. If that was the case, then Kishan should not have played. It was not a do-or-die game," he added.
"If he had a niggle, he could have been rested. India were already ahead 3-0."

stories.headline: 'Villa scam': IPS Prashakha Mathur now put on APO; IAS husband currently abroad
stories.deck: Rajasthan's government has placed IPS officer Prashakha Mathur on Awaiting Posting Order amid an inquiry linked to her husband, IAS officer Shikhar Agrawal. The probe, initiated by the Anti-Corruption Bureau, investigates allegations that Agrawal improperly assisted Goyal Fashions Pvt Ltd, garnering personal benefits. Evidence indicates the couple obtained villas at below-market prices in…
stories.bodyText:
JAIPUR: The Rajasthan government has placed IPS officer Prashakha Mathur on Awaiting Posting Order (APO), a day after the Anti-Corruption Bureau (ACB) opened a preliminary inquiry into allegations that her husband, senior IAS officer Shikhar Agrawal, misused his official position to favour a private company in return for benefits to himself and members of his family.
Mathur, a 1995-batch IPS officer, was serving as additional director general of police (ADGP), planning, modernisation and welfare, at police headquarters. Agrawal, a 1993-batch IAS officer, was serving as additional chief secretary, industries, when the state government placed him on APO on Wednesday.
Following Saturday’s action against Mathur, the ACB clarified that its ongoing inquiry is currently limited to Agrawal and allegations that he misused his official position to benefit hotels and resorts firm Goyal Fashions Pvt Ltd, causing losses to the state exchequer.
Although no formal inquiry has been announced against Mathur so far, sources in the ACB said the possibility of the agency expanding the scope of its inquiry to include her cannot be ruled out.
What are the allegations against Agrawal?
The bureau’s prima facie findings point to the couple purchasing dozens of villas from Goyal Fashions in Udaipur and Alwar at prices substantially below market value.
In return, the IAS officer is alleged to have colluded with the company’s directors and helped it secure undue financial benefits. 
These allegedly included relaxations in conditions governing resort construction, approvals without verification and a special concessional financial package.
The ACB argues that these benefits caused substantial financial losses to the state.
FIR may follow if allegations are substantiated
ACB officials said a formal FIR could be registered against Agrawal if the preliminary inquiry substantiates the allegations against him.
Sources close to the investigation said the bureau could also call Mathur in for questioning if warranted.
The ACB has not announced any formal inquiry against the IPS officer so far. The bureau has maintained that its ongoing probe is currently limited to Agrawal.
How did the ACB inquiry begin?
Chief secretary V Srinivas met ACB director general Govind Gupta on Friday. He later reiterated the state government's "zero tolerance" policy towards corruption in a post on X.
Following formal approval from the state government the same day, the ACB registered a preliminary inquiry against Agrawal.
The IAS officer is currently abroad and could be questioned upon his return, sources said.
What will the inquiry examine?
The inquiry is likely to examine a wide range of allegations, including misuse of official position and accumulation of assets disproportionate to known sources of income.
The ACB could register a formal FIR against Agrawal if the allegations against him are substantiated during the preliminary inquiry.

stories.headline: Taiwan says China harassing shipping with east coast patrol
stories.bodyText: Taipei: China's Coast Guard is harassing shipping with its latest patrol off Taiwan's east coast and trying to exert a fictional jurisdiction, the Taiwanese Coast Guard said, adding it had sent its own ships to keep watch. China, which views Taiwan as its own territory, has stepped up activity off the island's east coast since June with regular coast guard patrols. Officials in Taiwan, which rejects Beijing's sovereignty claims, say they believe China is practising for a potential maritime blockade using overlapping military, paramilitary and civilian assets. Taipei regards the area off its east coast as critical to wartime supply routes from allies in the event of a blockade or conflict. China recognises no claims of sovereignty by Taiwan. Responding late Saturday to China's announcement of its latest east coast patrol, Taiwan's Coast Guard said two Chinese ships were involved and it had sent its own forces to monitor. .Political affirmative action? Look to Taiwan. Chinese state media showed video of one of its ships broadcasting a radio message that it was carrying out law enforcement and offering help should any be needed. It did not say who the message was broadcast at, but showed footage of an unidentified fishing trawler. Taiwan's Coast Guard said China's "attempts to harass ships at sea through radio communications are a clear expansion of power that violate international law, undermine regional peace and stability, and deviate from reality". "Our country holds sovereign rights and jurisdiction over the exclusive economic zone east of Taiwan, and China has absolutely no jurisdiction over any of Taiwan's waters," it added. China on Saturday also sent another Coast Guard ship close to the Taiwan-controlled Pratas Islands, which are strategically located at the top of the South China Sea, Taiwan's Coast Guard said separately. Taiwan has so far this year "expelled" Chinese Coast Guard vessels from Pratas waters 13 times, it added. The Pratas have no permanent civilian population and lie roughly between southern Taiwan and Hong Kong. Security experts see them as vulnerable to Chinese attack due to their distance — more than 400 km (250 miles) — from Taiwan.

briefs.headline: 6.0-magnitude earthquake strikes Japan's coast near Shima
briefs.bodyText:
A magnitude 6.0 
earthquake
 struck 58 km southeast of Shima, off Japan's Mie Prefecture coast, early Sunday, according to the US Geological Survey (USGS). The quake's epicentre was also located around 110 km south-southeast of Tsu, the capital of Mie Prefecture, which has a population of over 250,000. The earthquake occurred at a depth of 352 km.
No 
tsunami warning
 was issued, and no immediate reports of damage or casualties were available.
Meanwhile, eyewitness accounts posted on the European-Mediterranean Seismological Centre (EMSC) website described the tremor as prolonged, with some reporting that the initial gentle shaking gradually grew stronger.
Further details are awaited.

briefs.headline: Armless archer Sheetal Devi wins double gold at Asian Para Games
briefs.deck: Sheetal Devi, born without arms, has developed a unique technique for archery using her feet, shoulder, and mouth. She was introduced to sports by the Indian Army and trained under Coach Kuldeep Vedwan. At the 2026 Asian Para Games, she won two gold medals and one silver, defending her previous titles successfully. Her achievements inspire children with disabilities to pursue sports and…
briefs.bodyText:
A bow is usually held with one hand and drawn with the other. For 
Sheetal Devi
, neither of those movements was an option. Born without arms, the young archer from Jammu and Kashmir had to find a way to make the equipment work with the body she had. Her answer was a technique that is now recognised around the world. She steadies the bow with her foot, uses her shoulder to draw the string and releases the arrow with the help of her mouth. It is a demanding combination of balance, strength and control. And it has taken years of practice to perfect.
Today, Devi is a Paralympic bronze medallist, a world champion and one of India's most celebrated para-archers. At the 2026 Asian Para Games in Aichi-Nagoya, Japan, she added another major achievement to her record, winning two gold medals and a silver. But the medals tell only part of the story. Her journey is also about learning a skill in an entirely different way, accepting setbacks and continuing to improve.
From everyday tasks to an unexpected sporting opportunity
Born on January 10, 2007, in Kishtwar district of Jammu and Kashmir, Sheetal grew up in the village of Loidhar. She learnt to perform everyday activities, including writing and eating, using her feet. These early experiences helped her develop the balance and control that would later become important in archery. 
Her sporting journey began to take shape after she was noticed at an Indian Army camp in 2019. The Army recognised her potential and helped her access educational and medical support. She eventually joined the Shri Mata Vaishno Devi Shrine Board Sports Complex in Katra, where she was introduced to sports.
Coach Kuldeep Vedwan played an important role in guiding her towards para-archery. The sport was not an obvious choice, given that conventional archery depends heavily on the use of both arms. Yet her coach and the training team worked with her to explore a method that suited her abilities.
At first, even lifting and controlling the bow was difficult. She had to build strength and learn how to coordinate different parts of her body. Training included resistance-band exercises, strength work and shooting at targets placed only a few metres away. With time, she developed the balance and control required to shoot at the standard competition distance of 50 metres. The process was gradual. Each practice session helped her understand what worked, what needed to change and how to make her movements more consistent.
A technique built through patience and practice
Sheetal's shooting style attracts attention because it looks very different from conventional archery. However, the technique is not a shortcut. It requires precise positioning, strong leg muscles, a stable body and careful control over every movement. She holds the bow with her foot and uses her shoulder to pull the string. A release aid held in her mouth helps her release the arrow. The sequence must be repeated with accuracy, even when the weather, wind or competition pressure makes shooting more difficult.
Her progress soon began to show in international competitions. At the 2023 Asian Para Games in Hangzhou, she won gold in the women's individual compound event and the mixed team event, along with a silver medal in women's doubles. She also won silver at the 2023 World Archery Para Championships. The next major milestone came at the Paris 2024 Paralympic Games. Partnering with Rakesh Kumar, she won bronze in the mixed team compound event. At 17, she became India's youngest Paralympic medallist. Although she missed an individual podium finish in Paris, the experience became another stage in her development.
In an interview with 
World Archery
 in October 2025, after winning the individual world title in Gwangju, South Korea, Sheetal spoke about the doubts she had faced. "I never paid attention to them; I just stayed focused on my game," she said. She also spoke about how rewarding it was to see young girls from distant places express an interest in taking up archery after watching her.
Two gold medals, one silver and a bigger message
Sheetal returned to the Asian Para Games in 2026 with the aim of defending the titles she had won in Hangzhou. She delivered two gold-medal performances in Japan, retaining the women's individual compound title and winning the compound mixed team event with Toman Kumar. She also earned silver in women's doubles with Payal Nag, completing a three-medal campaign.
Speaking to the Asian Paralympic Committee after the victories, she said, "I'm very happy – two gold medals and a silver in my second Asian Para Games. It feels all the hard work done in the past years was rewarded in one day. She also explained how she approached the pressure of the final: "I was just thinking to shoot my best; follow the process." It was a simple description of the focus that has shaped her career.
Her story has reached people well beyond the archery field. In a 2024 interview with World Archery, Sheetal spoke about receiving messages from children with disabilities who wanted to follow her example. She said she hoped more people would believe they could achieve something despite their disabilities. She also urged parents to support their children and recognise what they are capable of.
Sheetal shares updates through her Instagram account, 
@sheetal_archery
. The belief, along with the training and support she has received, has helped her build a career on her own terms. Her achievements are not simply a story of winning despite a physical condition. They are also a reminder that sporting skill is developed through technique, coaching, practice and the willingness to keep learning. For anyone watching her take aim, the arrow reaching the target may last only a moment. The work behind it has taken years.

briefs.headline: 23 years later: Pakistan recreate India's Lord's magic with record-equalling chase
briefs.deck: Pakistan produced a memorable run chase to beat Sri Lanka by three wickets in the One-Day International tri-series final in Lahore on Saturday. Fakhar Zaman led the charge with a brilliant century as the hosts chased down a target of 326 with nine balls to spare. Pakistan finished on 331 for seven in 48.3 overs to register the joint-highest successful chase in an ODI final. Pakistan equalled…
briefs.bodyText:
Pakistan produced a memorable run chase to beat Sri Lanka by three wickets in the One-Day International tri-series final in Lahore on Saturday. 
Fakhar Zaman
 led the charge with a brilliant century as the hosts chased down a target of 326 with nine balls to spare.
Pakistan finished on 331 for seven in 48.3 overs to register the joint-highest successful chase in an ODI final.
Pakistan equalled India's famous record against England in the 2002 NatWest Series final at Lord's.
The victory also ended Pakistan's long wait for an ODI tri-series title. They last won one in 2008, when they defeated India in the Kitply Cup final in Bangladesh.
Pakistan equal India's famous 2002 record
Pakistan's successful chase of 326 is now level with India's famous run chase against England in the 2002 NatWest Series final.
India had chased down England's target of 326 at Lord's to win the final by two wickets in one of the most memorable matches in their ODI history.
Mohammad Kaif
 played a match-winning unbeaten knock of 87, while 
Yuvraj Singh
 scored 69. The two shared a crucial partnership after India had lost five wickets with the team still needing plenty of runs.
Zaheer Khan and Kaif eventually took India home in a thrilling finish, with two runs needed from the final five balls. 
India completed the chase with three balls remaining.
More than two decades later, Pakistan matched that achievement with another successful chase of 326 in an ODI final.
Zaman leads Pakistan's chase with a century
Pakistan did not have the best start to their chase. Dilshan Madushanka struck twice in the powerplay, including the important wicket of Babar Azam, who departed for a five-ball duck.
However, Fakhar Zaman and Saad Baig brought Pakistan back into the contest with a 149-run partnership.
Baig scored 74 off 75 balls and registered his maiden ODI half-century before Maheesh Theekshana ended his innings.
Zaman continued to attack and brought up his 12th ODI century. He scored 127 off just 99 balls to keep Pakistan on course.
The left-hander also shared a quick 57-run stand with Salman Agha, who contributed 17 before Madushanka dismissed him.
Pakistan were reduced to 230 for five, but Arafat Minhas and Hasan Nawaz ensured there was no late collapse.
Minhas, Nawaz finish the job
With the match still in the balance, Minhas and Nawaz joined hands to put together a match-winning 94-run partnership.
Minhas scored a valuable half-century, providing the finishing push Pakistan needed after Zaman's dismissal.
The hosts eventually reached 331 for seven in 48.3 overs to complete a memorable victory in front of their home crowd.
Kamindu Mendis, Rathnayake power Sri Lanka to 325
Earlier, Sri Lanka posted a strong total of 325 for eight after being asked to bat first.
Kamindu Mendis was the star of their innings, scoring 131 off 128 balls. Pavan Rathnayake also played an important role with a fluent 77.
The two shared a 146-run partnership off 119 deliveries to put Sri Lanka in a strong position.
Kamindu brought up his maiden ODI century and struck 12 fours and two sixes during his impressive knock.
Sri Lanka had made a positive start, with Avishka Fernando and Kamindu adding 51 runs in the powerplay. Fernando's dismissal in the 18th over ended the opening partnership.
Pakistan captain Kusal Mendis also fell soon after, leaving Sri Lanka at 109 for two.
Pakistan bowlers fight back at the death
Just when Sri Lanka looked set for a total of more than 340, Pakistan's bowlers pulled things back in the final overs.
Shaheen Shah Afridi removed Dasun Shanaka and Rathnayake within two overs to put pressure on the visitors. Afridi finished with two wickets for 50 runs.
Sahan Arachchige added a quick 15 off 12 balls before Naseem Shah dismissed him.
Pakistan's late fightback restricted Sri Lanka to 325 for eight, a total that eventually proved insufficient against Zaman's century and the contributions from Minhas and Nawaz.
Pakistan end long wait for tri-series title
The victory gave Pakistan their first ODI tri-series title since 2008.
They also made amends for their defeat to New Zealand in the final of a home tri-series in 2025.
This time, Pakistan held their nerve in a high-scoring final and produced a historic chase to lift the trophy.

Who are the Indian-origin candidates in U.S. midterm elections?
briefs.deck: Democratic lawmakers Ro Khanna, Pramila Jayapal, Ami Bera and Suhas Subramanyam are seeking re-election to the U.S. Congress
briefs.bodyText:
Indian-origin candidates are seeking office across the United States in the November 3, 2026, midterm elections, the polls are so called because they fall midway through a President’s four-year term
All 435 seats in the House of Representatives are due for election, since members serve two-year terms. In the Senate, where members serve six years, 35 of the 100 seats are up for election, including special elections in Ohio and Florida.
The Indian-origin candidates are contesting from States including California, Washington, Virginia, Arizona, Florida, Texas, Ohio, New York and Maryland. Their races span different levels of government, from the U.S. Congress and State executive offices to city leadership positions.
Several Indian-Americans are in the fray across Texas, Florida, Arizona, Ohio, New York and Los Angeles. Democratic lawmakers Ro Khanna, Pramila Jayapal, Ami Bera and Suhas Subramanyam are seeking re-election to the U.S. Congress.
Here are some of the prominent Indian-origin candidates contesting the midterm elections:
Ro Khanna
Congressman Khanna is a member of the progressive wing of the Democratic Party. His grandfather, Amarnath Vidyalankar, was a freedom fighter who was imprisoned alongside Mahatma Gandhi and later served as a Congress Member of Parliament.
Mr. Khanna is a second-generation immigrant. His father, a chemical engineer from the Indian Institute of Technology, and his mother, a school teacher, migrated to the United States from Punjab. Born in Philadelphia, Mr. Khanna studied economics at the University of Chicago before earning a law degree from Yale Law School. He later worked as an intellectual property lawyer with clients from the technology sector.
A Democrat from California, Mr. Khanna is seeking re-election from California’s 17th Congressional District, which includes parts of Silicon Valley. He has criticised President Donald Trump’s policies as “utterly destructive”, described him as a “lame duck”, and said Democrats would prevail in the 2026 midterm elections and the 2028 presidential election.
Pramila Jayapal
Congresswoman Jayapal, who was born in Chennai, is seeking another term from Washington’s 7th Congressional District. In 2020, she became the second Indian-American woman elected to the U.S. House of Representatives.
Also read: Pramila Jayapal has a close Bengaluru connect
Ms. Jayapal traces her roots to Kerala. Her mother, Maya Jayapal, is a writer and counsellor and the author of Bangalore: Roots and Beyond.
Ms. Jayapal was the first Indian-American woman elected to the U.S. House of Representatives and has represented Washington’s 7th Congressional District since 2017.
On October 14, 2026, Ms. Jayapal voiced concern over reports about the removal of 13 crore names from draft electoral rolls in India. The Democratic lawmaker said she supported non-violent protests against what she described as anti-democratic efforts.
She said the developments appeared similar to attempts in the United States to undermine voting rights. India rejected her remarks on the Election Commission’s revision of electoral rolls, describing them as unwarranted, uninformed and an interference in the electoral practices of a fellow democracy.
Ami Bera
Dr. Bera, a physician and politician serving in the U.S. House of Representatives, is seeking re-election as the Democratic candidate from California’s 3rd Congressional District.
The son of Gujarati immigrants from Rajkot, Dr. Bera was born in the United States. He was the third Indian-American elected to Congress. His father, Babulal Bera, later pleaded guilty to illegally funding his son’s election campaigns in 2010 and 2012.
Also read | Congressman Ami Bera’s father guilty of election crime
Dr. Bera has consistently advocated stronger India-U.S. ties. He served as co-chair of the Congressional Caucus on India and Indian Americans during the 114th Congress from January 2015 to January 2017.
Suhas Subramanyam
Congressman Subramanyam, who made history by becoming the first Indian-American elected to Congress from Virginia and the East Coast in 2024, is seeking re-election.
Mr. Subramanyam’s parents moved to the United States through Dulles Airport in the late 1970s. His mother is from Bengaluru and his father from Chennai, though he also spent part of his childhood in Secunderabad because his father served in the military.
Mr. Subramanyam has strongly supported closer India-U.S. ties, describing India as one of the world’s most important democracies and stressing the importance of strong relations between democratic nations.
Vivek Ramaswamy
Republican Vivek Ramaswamy is running for Ohio Governor. Backed by President Donald Trump, Mr. Ramaswamy won the Republican primary in May and became the party’s nominee for the November election.
A former co-chair of the Department of Government Efficiency (DOGE), Mr. Ramaswamy launched a presidential campaign in 2024 before withdrawing and endorsing Mr. Trump.
The son of immigrants from Kerala, Mr. Ramaswamy was born in Cincinnati, Ohio. His father, Vadakanchery Ganapathy Ramaswamy, worked as an engineer at General Electric, while his mother is a psychiatrist.
Mr. Ramaswamy studied at Harvard University and Yale Law School before building a career in biotechnology and finance. He founded Roivant Sciences and served as its chief executive officer from 2014 to 2021. He later founded the asset management firm Strive. According to Forbes, his net worth is estimated at $2.5 billion.
Saritha Komatireddy
Republican Saritha Komatireddy, the party’s nominee for New York Attorney General, is a former federal prosecutor and a graduate of Harvard College and Harvard Law School.
She spent more than a decade prosecuting members of Al Qaeda, ISIS and Mexican drug cartels. As a federal prosecutor in the Eastern District of New York, she handled several high-profile cases involving terrorism, cybercrime, narcotics trafficking, money laundering, fraud and foreign public corruption, according to her official campaign website.
She later served in senior positions including Chief of International Narcotics and Money Laundering, Deputy Chief of Appeals and Deputy Chief of General Crimes in the district’s National Security and Cybercrime Section. She also served as Chief of Staff at the Drug Enforcement Administration and is currently a partner at Holtzman Vogel.
Nithya Raman
Nithya Raman, an urban planner and member of the Los Angeles City Council representing District 4, is contesting the Los Angeles mayoral election, according to the City of Los Angeles official website.
A graduate of Harvard University and the Massachusetts Institute of Technology, Ms. Raman has served as co-chair of the Silver Lake Neighborhood Council’s Homelessness Committee and co-founded the SELAH Neighbourhood Homeless Coalition.
She was elected to the City Council in 2020, becoming the first Asian-American woman and the first South Asian elected to the body. In March 2024, she won a second term.
Ms. Raman currently chairs the Civil Rights, Immigration, Social Services and Neighbourhoods Committee and serves on several other council committees.
Pooja Sethi
Pooja Sethi is the Democratic candidate for Texas House District 47. An attorney by profession, Ms. Sethi has served as chief of staff in the Texas Legislature and as chair of the Travis County Democratic Party, according to her Linkedin profile.
Sandeep Srivastava
Sandeep Srivastava is the Democratic candidate for Texas House District 66. A long-time resident of the Plano-Frisco area, businessman and community advocate, Mr. Srivastava is challenging a five-term Republican incumbent in the November election, according to his official campaign website.
Pia Dandiya
Pia Dandiya, a former high school principal, is the Democratic candidate from Florida’s 22nd Congressional District and faces Republican Casey Askar.
A first-generation American, Ms. Dandiya has built her campaign around education and affordability. Born and raised in Palm Beach County, she began her career as a teacher before becoming a high school principal in Harlem.
She later founded a high school aimed at improving opportunities for low-income students. According to her campaign, every graduate of the school secured admission to college despite a large majority coming from low-income households.
Amish Shah
Amish Shah, a physician and former State Representative, is the Democratic candidate from Arizona’s 1st Congressional District. He is contesting against Republican candidate Jay Feely, a former National Football League kicker endorsed by President Donald Trump.
Mr. Shah served three terms in the Arizona House of Representatives. He narrowly lost the 2024 congressional election to Republican David Schweikert.
The Cook Political Report has classified Arizona’s 1st Congressional District as “Lean Democratic”, making the contest one of the closely watched races of the election cycle.

stories.headline: HMT brings out new ‘Kannadiga’ watch collection for Karnataka
stories.deck: These watches have Kannada numericals, a Gandabherunda emblem, a yellow-red Kannada flag and the series name “HMT Kannadiga”, in Kannada letters.
stories.bodyText:
In what comes as music to the ears of watch aficionados, Hindustan Machine Tools (HMT) will unveil a new collection of watches named “HMT Kannadiga” on the occasion of the 71st Kannada Rajyotsava.
These watches have Kannada numericals, a Gandabherunda emblem, a yellow-red Kannada flag and the series name “HMT Kannadiga”, in Kannada letters.
Union Minister H.D. Kumaraswamy on Saturday announced that the watches would be available in two variants — strap and chain — and four different styles. They are estimated to cost ₹3,500 and ₹3,600, respectively. With this price range, the new collection will join HMT’s premium watch segment.
According to officials, the watches will feature modern technology and a radium glow. The strap variants will be fitted with genuine Italian leather straps, each costing ₹450, he added. The unveiling will be held at the HMT Grounds in north Bengaluru on Sunday evening.
Soon after the announcement, social media platforms were flooded with posts about the new collection, reflecting the widespread public interest. Several social media groups also saw discussions about the new collection, its price range, and the timing of its release.
It may be recalled that a queue stretching nearly a kilometre formed when the Gandaberunda collection, another popular Kannada watch, was restocked on Independence Day earlier this year. Within hours, the collection was sold out. It will be back in stock shortly, sources said.
Suman T., an HMT watch enthusiast, said the company was coming up with a new collection after a long time and that it would undoubtedly sell out soon. “The PSU should consider manufacturing in bulk, especially models such as Gandabherunda and Roman, which are widely discussed in several watch enthusiast groups,” he said.
Addressing the media in New Delhi, Mr. Kumaraswamy said the initiative was a special contribution to Karnataka on the occasion of the 71st Rajyotsava. “HMT, popularly known as ‘India’s timekeeper’ and a source of pride for Karnataka, has always made a special contribution to the state’s language, culture, and heritage, despite being a central government undertaking,” he said.

stories.headline: On Karnataka Rajyotsava, a digital archive of 220 documentaries captures State’s many worlds
stories.deck: The documentaries, spanning 1982 to 2026, capture 117 places across 94 hours of viewing and have been catalogued by regions and themes such as communities, music and art, livelihoods, politics and protest, and so on.
stories.bodyText:
Varun Nagesh, a Bengaluru-based marketer who hails from Shivamogga, calls himself a documentary freak. So, when he decided to make a contribution to mark 70 years since the formation of the Mysore State, renamed Karnataka in 1973, the choice was pretty obvious: a dedicated website which brings together 220 documentaries on Karnataka, capturing the land that is “one State, many worlds”.
The documentaries, spanning 1982 to 2026, capture 117 places across 94 hours of viewing and have been catalogued by regions and themes such as communities, music and art, livelihoods, politics and protest, and so on.
Understanding the diversities
For Mr. Nagesh, the idea of the project originated from “a sense of being South Indian and a Kannadiga”.
“As you grow older, you begin to understand why certain things are important to maintain social harmony and structures,” he said. According to him, the idea was to create awareness that Kannada and Karnataka exist in many forms.
There is no single, fixed version of Kannada. The language has evolved into different dialects, with influences from other languages, he pointed out, citing the example of ‘Aravu Kannada’, a dialect spoken in parts of Bengaluru, which has influences from Telugu, Tamil and Kannada.
“That is the beauty of this diversity. Unity in diversity can endure only when the diversity is recognised. Otherwise, it becomes a struggle over who gets to define that unity,” he said.
Portals to layers of history
But why documentaries?
“Because documentaries involve going to a place, capturing footage and building a story around what has actually happened. You cannot change the scene simply because you want to as a director,” explained Mr. Nagesh.
A staunch believer that people should explore different perspectives and understand the social context rather than use history to prove how knowledgeable they are or to attack someone else, he pointed out that Karnataka’s history has several layers.
For him, documentaries are the perfect portals to discover these layers.
“I built it because I enjoy watching these documentaries. It is almost like a time machine that takes you back to another era,” he said.
The roots of the idea stemmed on a Saturday when he sought documentary recommendations from a Kannada movie community. Despite the number of community members being in thousands, the number of Kannada documentary recommendations he got was just 10-15. Most documentaries were scattered across the internet and difficult to discover.
“That made me realise that there could be others who wanted to discover such content but didn’t know where to look. So, I built the website for myself and for them,” he stated.
Mr. Nagesh plans to make the website an open-source platform where people can contribute.
“I don’t want the website to reflect only my perspective. I’d like people to have healthy discussions and debates about history, without them turning toxic,” he said, adding, “I feel people should learn about their history not to feel superior to others or use it to attack them, but to feel humbled. We should draw confidence, not rage, from that pride.”

stories.headline: I see this Rajyotsava Award as a recognition for Karnataka's artisans and textile heritage: Prasad Bidapa
stories.bodyText:
Fashion Guru and textile revivalist Prasad Bidapa, who has been honoured with the Karnataka Rajyotsava Award this year for his contribution to fashion, sees the recognition as an opportunity to draw attention to the state’s rich textile and artisanal heritage. He believes Karnataka’s silks, cottons and traditional crafts have the potential to become global luxury products, provided they receive sustained government support. In a conversation with us, he discusses the need to revive traditional weaving, build brands around local crafts and place Karnataka’s textiles on international fashion runways.
Fashion has rarely received recognition in state honours. Does this award mark a breakthrough for the industry?
A lot has happened in textile heritage revival over the years. Great people such as Pupul Jayakar and Kamaladevi Chattopadhyay have worked on it, but the sector is still not where it should be. Globally, Indian textiles are considered luxury because they are handmade. If we define luxury as handmade, everything we produce by hand in India should come under the luxury sector. Yet, in the end, brands such as Chanel and Dior benefit from this space, while we have not managed to do enough ourselves.
 Without government support, it is very difficult to change that.
Even initiatives such as 
Swadesh
, backed by the Ambanis, address only a small percentage of India's artisanal community. If the government takes textiles seriously, it can transform the lives of a significant section of the population. Textiles are not just about spinning and weaving. The industry encompasses cotton farming, silk rearing, processing, printing, dyeing, retail and much more. Imagine the scale of employment and economic activity it can generate.
Is the Rajyotsava Award likely to put greater responsibility on you to drive this change?
I hope it opens doors and encourages the government to listen to the programmes and projects we have developed for silk revival, Dharwad cotton and other wonderful textile traditions. Why can't we create globally recognised products using Karnataka's traditional textiles and crafts? There is nothing particularly difficult about it. We need the right support.
You cannot expect the private sector to shoulder this responsibility entirely because it ultimately becomes a profit-and-loss question. The government can invest in making weavers and artisans into brands, improving their livelihoods and giving their products a global platform. You do not have to hold their hands for 20 years. Support them for three or four years, help them build a strong foundation, and they can take it forward themselves.
What would it take to bring Karnataka's traditional textiles to international fashion runways?
We need to ask ourselves what our designers are thinking about. We should be using our artisans and making it compulsory for Indian designers to use Indian textiles rather than relying on Chinese imports. There is so much rubbish in the market when we have such extraordinary craftsmanship of our own.
Karnataka has incredible textile and craft traditions. Look at Bidriware, Channapatna toys and the many other crafts the state is known for. The potential is mind-blowing. With the right support, we can take these traditions to an entirely different level.
How can Karnataka leverage its textile heritage to create economic opportunities?
Karnataka, more than almost any other state, has the potential to do this because we are the cradle of silk. Mulberry silk from Karnataka has reached every other part of the country, but look at the state of our own silk industry today. If you travel along the silk route through Ramanagara, Channapatna, Srirangapatna and Mandya, you see very little of the activity that should be happening. These places should be buzzing. The government needs to take up the revival of the sector on a war footing, working with the textile and tourism departments.
For instance, we could have created a tourism experience around the silk route, attracting Japanese visitors in particular. Groups of hundreds could travel from Bengaluru to Mysuru, experiencing how silk is reared, spun and woven. The Japanese love these textiles. Such an initiative could become a significant tourism attraction.
Our tourism numbers are low. Sri Lanka, which is comparable in size to a single Indian state, attracts more tourists than we do. Textiles are not just an industry; they are a metaphor for Indian luxury, rarity and skills that have survived for thousands of years. We need to monetise and promote this heritage.
On a personal level, does this award feel like validation of the work you have done over the years?
For me, this award is representative. It is not about me; it is about the entire sector receiving recognition. I hope the government will now take up the cause with greater urgency, listen to the projects being developed across the country and help transform this wonderful sector into a global sensation.
Karnataka, especially, can make this happen. We have silk, and the Japanese are keen to buy our saris. The world today is flooded with synthetic silk, much of it polyester-based, and people often cannot tell the difference. Even traditional Kanjeevaram and Banarasi saris are being replicated in polyester. When a genuine sari costs Rs 40,000 and an imitation is available for Rs 5,000, many buyers will naturally choose the cheaper option. We need to fight this. How can we allow a 3,500-year-old tradition to be cheapened like that?
I want this to become an opportunity to promote Karnataka's textiles and crafts, create globally recognised products and improve the lives of the people who make them. We have the skills, the heritage and the raw material. We have everything needed to make this happen.

stories.headline: Students set example of conservation at park clean-up drives in Bengaluru
stories.bodyText:
Bengaluru
: Students and citizens continued to come together for Bengaluru’s neighbourhood parks Saturday under the Times Of India’s #IamBengaluru – Volunteer for Parks, presented by Multigen, in association with Kristu Jayanti University and supported by the Greater Bengaluru Authority (GBA).

This initiative gives students an opportunity to turn that concern into action, and I hope more people will come forward to volunteer at lakes and other public spaces.”
B Sreenadh, software engineer, Cognizant; Nagawara resident, recalled, “I remember Bengaluru’s parks as much greener when I was growing up, but the city’s expansion is changing that landscape. We need citizens to give a few hours each week to protect our community parks.”

I love walking and running in parks, and they give me a lot of energy.”
Ishan, Class 10, Team Evara, NPS Rajajinagar said he has always loved spending time in its parks. “Cleaning the park today made me happy, and I hope initiatives like #IamBengaluru can help bring Bengaluru back to how it used to be.”

Parks should be places where people come to relax and connect with nature, not avoid because of litter and dirt. I wanted to do my part so that everyone who visit after us feels happy to be here.”
Tisha, degree student, MESA College, said, “Lalbagh and Cubbon Park were among the first things I heard about when I came to Bengaluru, and they became part of how I experienced the city. briefs.headline: Karnataka Historical Atlas: From temples to battles, state’s past comes alive on digital map
briefs.bodyText:
Bengaluru:
 What connects a temple in a small Karnataka village to a dynasty that ruled centuries ago? Where did historical battles take place, and how did Karnataka’s kingdoms connect with the rest of the world? A new digital platform developed in Bengaluru aims to help people explore such questions through an interactive map of the state’s history.
Called Karnataka Ithihasa Bhoopata (Karnataka Historical Atlas), the Kannada-first digital public history initiative allows users to navigate Karnataka’s past through maps, timelines and curated historical resources. Developed by Sanchaya, a non-profit initiative working at the intersection of the Kannada language, technology and cultural preservation, the portal brings together information on kingdoms, rulers, inscriptions, monuments, literature, the freedom movement, district histories and cultural life.
Users can explore the atlas through several categories, including dynastic maps and timelines, guided historical story routes, Karnataka’s global connections, geography and natural history, prominent personalities such as kings, poets and thinkers, and the freedom movement and its leaders.
The map itself uses distinct markers to identify historical sites and resources, making it easier for users to locate temples, inscriptions, royal emblems and artefacts, battle sites, monuments, forts, palaces, museums, archives, libraries and historical gardens. 
It also maps references to other states, offering a glimpse into Karnataka’s historical connections beyond its present-day geographical boundaries.
“The portal is a little more than just a map to tell stories. It contains verifiable and citable resources from various sources,” said Omshivaprakash HL, founder of Sanchaya.
The platform draws on historical publications and official records, including Epigraphia Indica, Carnatica, various volumes of Ithihasa Darsha published by Karnataka Itihasa Academy, and books digitised through Sanchaya’s other initiative, Servants of Knowledge. Records are accompanied by sources and their review status, wherever available.
The idea, Omshivaprakash said, is to help users understand how a place, person, inscription, literary work or historical event relates to a particular period and region, rather than merely memorising dates. Schools and colleges can use the atlas for history and social science lessons, district history projects, heritage walks, quizzes and research assignments.
Founded in 2010, Sanchaya has been working towards making Kannada literary and historical resources accessible through technology and digitisation. Karnataka Historical Atlas is an open-source, open-data and open-knowledge initiative, inviting students, researchers, teachers, educational institutions and members of the public to contribute. “This entire project is an open-source initiative in Kannada. It also has an English interface. We’ve received requests to introduce other languages too,” he said.
Describing the atlas as an ongoing experiment, Omshivaprakash said public feedback, corrections and additional historical sources would help improve it. “The atlas is intended as a research and learning companion, not as a replacement for prescribed textbooks,” he added.
Karnataka Historical Atlas can be accessed at https://karnata.sanchaya.net.

briefs.headline: Curd price hike is Karnataka Milk Federation’s call, says chief minister DK Shivakumar
briefs.bodyText:
Chief minister 
DK Shivakumar
 distanced his govt from the curd hike, saying the decision was taken by Karnataka Milk Federation, which sets rates by fat content.
“We intervened only in the price of milk. As far as other factors are concerned, if the fat content is higher, a corresponding rate is fixed and the price goes up accordingly,” he told mediapersons.
‘We need to show respect to Gomata’
Defending the milk price hike, Shivakumar said: “If we want to protect our cows, we must provide them with good food. To provide them with food, we need fodder. For fodder to be available, farmers must have money in their hands. Otherwise, production will keep declining. We must do our part to show respect to Gomata and protect cattle.”
He said producers had sought Rs 12 and the cabinet cleared Rs 8 on Thursday. Toned milk will now cost Rs 54 a litre and Shubham Rs 60. “Prices are much higher in neighbouring states, and farmers in 
Karnataka
 were moving their milk to those states. Milk availability is declining as well. Due to 
drought
, milk production has come down,” he said.
The CM’s office countered with data showing Nandini remains cheaper than private brands. As of Sept 12, its curd sold at Rs 54 a litre against a private average of Rs 68.4. Toned milk at Rs 46 was well below the Rs 52.8 average, while full-cream Samruddhi at Rs 55 was up to Rs 19 cheaper than rivals. The study also proposes revising prices periodically on the basis of fat and solid-not-fat content, as private dairies do, so that cooperative unions do not bear losses.
``Karnataka has a total of 28.8 lakh dairy farmers, of whom 67 per cent of KMF members are small and marginal farmers. This decision is a significant step towards providing fair remuneration for their hard work, especiolaly in times of drought,” Shivakumar addedd. “Our government is committed to both protecting the interests of farmers and ensuring the supply of quality milk to consumers at affordable prices,” Shivakumar said.
Union minister Pralhad Joshi pounced on the hike, accusing the govt of using KMF to cover fiscal mismanagement and depleted coffers. “While giving curd to the people, the Congress govt is enjoying the butter,” he said, adding that the increases would hit poor and middle-class families hardest.

briefs.headline: Ranya Rao’s temple visit in protocol vehicle raises questions in Karnataka
briefs.bodyText:
Hassan:
 Actress 
Ranya Rao
, out on bail in a gold smuggling case, visited Hasanamba temple here Saturday with her family in a protocol vehicle accompanied by police personnel, raising questions about the arrangements made for the visit.
Ranya travelled from the govt guest house to the temple with her father, retired DGP Ramachandra Rao, and other family members. Protocol staff and police personnel accompanied them.
Protocol officer V Manjunath, however, said the vehicle was registered in the name of Ramachandra Rao and its use was in accordance with prescribed arrangements. “Five people, including him, were permitted to travel to and from the temple in the vehicle. His family members were given the facility. There is no question of any violation of protocol,” he said.
As Ranya approached the temple, media personnel tried to question and photograph her. She gestured to indicate that she would not respond and proceeded for darshan. Ranya was arrested in March 2025 at Kempegowda International Airport in Bengaluru after arriving from Dubai. She was later detained under the Conservation of Foreign Exchange and Prevention of Smuggling Activities Act and spent over a year in prison before securing bail.

briefs.headline: Bengaluru-Goa Vande Bharat train via Mangaluru from November third week
briefs.bodyText:
Bengaluru: Karnataka is set to receive yet another Vande Bharat train later this month – connecting Bengaluru and Madgaon via Mangaluru. The train traversing through Konkan route will take around 13 hours to reach the Goan terminal.
Railway officials said the train could be flagged off in the third week of Nov, though an exact date is yet to be finalised. The railway ministry Saturday notified the introduction of train number 26655/26656, which will operate from Yeshwantpur. It will run six days a week, departing from Yeshwantpur at 7:35 am except Wednesdays.
In the return direction, the service will originate from Madgaon at 8:20 am and reach Yeshwantpur by 9:15 pm. The service will not operate from Madgaon on Thursdays.
After its introduction, the railways will discontinue the Madgaon-Mangaluru Vande Bharat. 
IRCTC
 has stopped ticket reservations for it from Nov 29.
The new Vande Bharat service will have 12 stoppages. It will halt at Shravanabelagola, Hassan, Sakaleshpura, Subrahmanya Road, Kabaka Puttur, Mangaluru Jn, Udupi, Kundapura, Mookambika Road Byndoor, Murdeshwar, Gokarna Road and Karwar.
Fastest rail link to coast
The Bengaluru-Mangaluru route, a high-footfall corridor in Karnataka, will have the benefit of higher priority through Vande Bharat. It will reach Mangaluru in less than eight hours, faster than any other train on the route.
However, speed restrictions will continue to be active along the electrified ghat section between Sakaleshpura and Subrahmanya Road. Despite having the capacity to travel at higher speeds, safety restrictions will limit the semi-high-speed express to just 30 kmph while covering the 55 km stretch.
During an initial trial, South Western Railway did not plan a stop at Kabaka Puttur. However, persistent passenger demand has led to its approval now.

briefs.headline: Only 25% done, Bengaluru’s Silk Board drain upgrade aims to end flooding before next monsoon
briefs.bodyText:
Bengaluru:
 The city’s chronically flood-prone Silk Board Junction may finally get a long-term drainage solution before the next monsoon, but only about a quarter of the ambitious stormwater drain upgrade has been completed so far.
Greater Bengaluru Authority (GBA) has set a target of finishing the remaining work of the World Bank-funded project within the next three months.
An official said the Rs 5-crore project involves constructing a 60-metre-long drain. Once completed, it is expected to carry nearly three times the volume of water handled by the existing system.
According to officials, the existing central drain is about 25 feet wide and 2.5 feet deep. Under the upgrade, it will be widened to nearly 50 feet and increased to a depth of around three metres.
However, during a field inspection Saturday, Bengaluru development minister Krishna Byre Gowda was informed that increasing the carrying capacity at Silk Board could potentially create bottlenecks downstream. Officials noted that drains along parts of HSR Layout and the Outer Ring Road have a lower carrying capacity and may face flooding during heavy rain if the upstream flow increases significantly.
Addressing the concern, Gowda directed B-Smile officials to examine whether drain-capacity enhancement works along the HSR and Outer Ring Road stretches could be incorporated into the ongoing Rs 400-crore Outer Ring Road redevelopment project.
Progress on the Silk Board works has been affected by ongoing Namma Metro construction. GBA officials said work at certain locations has been paused to avoid clashes with Metro-related activities, which are currently being prioritised.
Despite the delay, officials said efforts are being made to prevent flooding by ensuring existing drains remain free of blockages.
Silk Board Junction has repeatedly witnessed flooding during heavy rain, often triggering massive traffic snarls.
Ward One campaign inaugurated
The minister also symbolically launched the ‘Ward One’ campaign at Silk Board Junction by initiating the painting of flyover pillars. The campaign is being rolled out across 43 wards under the five municipal corporations of GBA, focusing on improving major junctions, public spaces and neighbourhood infrastructure.
Free-left access to ease traffic congestion
To improve traffic movement from Electronics City towards BTM Layout, the minister directed officials to explore the possibility of installing a steel grid over a section of the stormwater drain at Silk Board Junction
to facilitate a free-left turn for vehicles.
He also instructed officials to examine the construction of a pedestrian walkway alongside the drain.
Officials said covering the drain and making the space accessible to pedestrians is not part of the original project design. However, following the minister’s suggestion, they would study the proposal.

briefs.headline: ED attaches assets worth ₹427 crore in ₹2,459-crore Belagavi Ponzi scam
briefs.deck: Over 35,000 investors allegedly cheated; properties of kingpin Shivanand Neelannavar, family members and associates attached
briefs.bodyText:
The Directorate of Enforcement (ED) has provisionally attached movable and immovable assets worth ₹427.16 crore belonging to Shivanand Siddappa Neelannavar, the alleged kingpin of a mega Ponzi scheme in Belagavi, and persons and entities associated with him.
The attachment order was issued by the ED’s Mangaluru Sub-Zonal Office on Friday under the Prevention of Money Laundering Act (PMLA), 2002, in connection with an alleged investment fraud involving proceeds of crime of approximately ₹2,459 crore.
The properties attached include fixed deposits, bank balances, share market holdings, agricultural land, bungalows and bookings of apartments in residential projects.
The ED investigation revealed that substantial portions of the collected money were diverted into high-risk stock market trading, resulting in net losses of ₹185.95 crore. Around ₹25 crore was allegedly routed through Shreemata Co-operative Credit Society Ltd. and Dhanashree Multipurpose Co-operative Society Ltd. to create fixed deposits, which were subsequently used as security for loans taken in the names of associates to purchase land.
The funds were also allegedly diverted to the bank accounts of close family members, including his wife Sangeeta and minor son Siddhant, besides being invested in business ventures such as Shivam Sevaa (OPC) Pvt. Ltd., which allegedly received ₹19 crore, Shivam Lifeline Pvt. Ltd. and Shivam Foods.
The ED identified 42 immovable properties, including agricultural plots, family bungalows and apartment bookings, along with financial assets held by the accused and associated entities.
Neelannavar was arrested on August 13, 2026. On October 9, the ED filed a prosecution complaint before the PMLA court in Mangaluru, seeking prosecution of five accused persons and entities, including Neelannavar .Further investigation is under way.

stories.headline: Windfall gains tax on diesel, ATF exports up; petrol cut to nil
stories.bodyText:
NEW DELHI: Govt Saturday increased the windfall gains tax on exports of diesel and jet fuel (ATF), while slashing the levy to zero on petrol for the fortnight beginning Oct 31.
There is no change in excise duty on petrol and diesel for domestic consumption.
According to a notification issued by the finance ministry, the rate of special additional excise duty (SAED) on diesel exports has been increased to Rs 11.5 a litre from Rs 8.5 a litre, while it has been marginally raised to Rs 11 per litre from Rs 10.5 a litre on ATF exports. The duty on petrol exports has been slashed to nil from Rs 2.5 per litre for the next fortnight.
The windfall tax - comprising SAED and road and infrastructure cess - on exports of petrol, diesel and ATF was introduced on March 27 to ensure domestic availability of petroleum products by discouraging overseas sales amid the West Asia crisis. The rates are determined by the average international prices of crude oil, petrol, diesel and ATF prevailing since the last review.

stories.headline: AAIB for better coordination between civil, defence aviation authorities
stories.bodyText:
NEW DELHI: The Aircraft Accident Investigation Bureau (AAIB) has sought a greater collaboration between civil aviation and defence authorities as a number of airports where commercial flights operate are defence airfields. Submitting its final report in a case at the Navy’s Dabolim Airport in Goa where an Air India Express flight and a Naval aircraft had ended up on the same runway at the same time, the AAIB has sought the establishment of “a formal framework for collaboration between DGCA/AAIB and defence on a priority basis” to ensure exchange of unclassified information and evidence for investigation of an incident or accident.
On April 3, 2026, a scheduled flight of AI Express was to take off from Dabolim for Delhi. Due to misunderstanding and miscommunication between the flight deck and ATC, it entered an active runway when a Naval “fighter was rolling” and the incident was a “near miss”. “On seeing the Navy aircraft at lift off, in the opposite direction the pilot-in-command of AI Express 1109 mentioned to the trainee first officer that the fighter did a low pass, as per the cockpit flight recorder recording,” says the report.
In its safety recommendations, AAIB has asked the Airports Authority of India (AAI) “to issue a circular to sensitise air traffic controllers for emphasising the use of standard phraseology and to review the use of phrases like ‘expect backtrack’ by ground controllers which can be easily misinterpreted as ‘enter backtrack’. ATCOs must listen carefully to the read-back and correct any factual error or any apparent misunderstanding.”
The investigator has asked a taxiway of Dabolim airport to be “considered as a hotspot due to its proximity with bays of civil apron and increased probability of the risk of potential ground collisions and runway incursions.”
The Navy has been advised to “publish installation of stop bars and their usage at Dabolim airport (and it may) consider establishing a standard frequency change over procedure for civil traffic transitioning from the ground frequency to the tower frequency, in order to avoid recurring confusion regarding the appropriate frequency to be used.”
The crew of the AI Express flight has been asked to “undergo counselling and pilot-in-command to undergo training on the safety lapses that resulted in the runway incursion due to lack of operational clarity and communication miss outs.” The airline has to issue a circular to “sensitise all crew for the lapses encountered in this occurrence.”

stories.headline: Centre releases additional instalment of tax devolution of ₹1.09 lakh crore to states
stories.deck: This is in addition to the regular monthly devolution and the second additional instalment this financial year
stories.bodyText:
The Centre on Saturday (October 31, 2026) released an additional instalment of tax devolution to state governments totalling over ₹1.09 lakh crore.
This is in addition to the regular monthly devolution and the second additional instalment this financial year.

"This release is in view of the upcoming festive season and to enable states to accelerate capital spending, and also to finance their development/welfare related expenditure," the Ministry said.

stories.headline: SEBI chairman says market regulator keeping eye on Tata Group developments
stories.deck: The comments came amid differences over governance matters at Tata Sons
stories.bodyText:
SEBI Chairman Tuhin Kanta Pandey on Saturday (October 31, 2026) said the market regulator is monitoring developments relating to governance at the holding company level in the Tata Group, and pointed out that the group's listed companies and their promoters are subject to SEBI's disclosure and compliance norms.
The comments came amid differences over governance matters at Tata Sons, the group's holding company, including the reappointment of N Chandrasekaran as chairman and the question of its proposed listing.
"At the holding company level, there are some issues, as that's not really a listed company. The rest of the companies, those which are listed, follow all the LODR (Listing Obligations and Disclosure Requirements) norms," Pandey told reporters on the sidelines of the launch of the Bharat Chamber Investors Forum.
These listed companies and promoters of those firms are subject to all norms, he said.
Asked whether the SEBI was keeping track of Tata Group's developments, he said, "Yes... I mean in the sense of, you know, we have to keep monitoring all the developments."
Mr. Pandey did not refer to any specific governance violation or regulatory action against the group in his remarks.
The Tata Group has 26 publicly listed companies, with a combined market capitalisation of$328 billion as of March 31, 2025, according to its FY25 annual report.
Of these, seven listed companies collectively hold around 11.92% in Tata Sons, according to an analysis by governance advisory firm InGovern. The firms also have more than 1.77 crore shareholder or folio accounts.
The seven companies are Tata Steel, Tata Motors Passenger Vehicles, Tata Chemicals, Tata Power, Indian Hotels, Tata Consumer Products and Tata Investment Corporation.
These companies are part of the group's larger portfolio of 26 listed entities and represent only those firms identified in the analysis as holding a stake in Tata Sons.
Tata Trusts holds around 66% in Tata Sons, while the Shapoorji Pallonji Group holds approximately 18.4%.

briefs.headline: Indigenous bullet train B28 undergoes 'squeeze test'
briefs.bodyText:
NEW DELHI: New Delhi: The country’s first indigenous high-speed train, B28, has undergone the vehicle body shell test, also known as the “squeeze test”, an important safety assessment to determine whether a train’s car body can withstand heavy external forces and pressure without excessive deformation or structural failure in case of a collision or crash.
The test was conducted at BEML’s production facility in Bengaluru. The central PSU is manufacturing the first two of indigenous bullet trains, each comprising eight coaches. The trains have been designed for an operating speed of 249 kmph and a testing speed of 275 kmph, as per a BEML tender document.
People aware of the development said the squeeze test is crucial as the trains will operate at high speeds and their car bodies must be capable of withstanding heavy forces in the event of a collision or accident.
“After the successful completion of this test, the prototype should ideally be ready in less than six months. Since the B28 (Bharat 28) train is not being built on Japanese Shinkansen technology, the development process should not take much time. The squeeze test establishes whether the body retains its shape under pressure and whether the passenger compartment maintains its structural integrity,” an official said.
The railways plans to begin trial runs of B28 on the 100-km Surat-Vapi section of the Ahmedabad-Mumbai High Speed Rail corridor by May-June 2027. Commercial operations on this stretch are scheduled to begin in August 2027.
While seeking Cabinet approval for the escalated cost of the country’s first bullet train project, the railway ministry had stated that two prototype trains were expected to be ready for trial runs in the first quarter of 2027. It had also said that the entire Gujarat section of the corridor was expected to be completed by December 2027, while the full 508-km Mumbai-Ahmedabad High Speed Rail corridor is targeted for completion by December 2030.

briefs.headline: IOC says crude Q2 price volatile as procurement swings between discounts and premiums
briefs.deck: Anuj Jain, Director (Finance) at Indian Oil also stated under-recoveries on LPG is projected at ₹309/cylinder in November and ₹370/cylinder in December.
briefs.bodyText:
Crude oil procurement remained volatile during the September quarter, with Indian Oil Corporation (IOC) sourcing supplies at discounts of up to $5 per barrel and premiums of as much as $12, Anuj Jain, Director (Finance), told investors during a post-results call on Saturday.
The Delhi-headquartered refiner’s net profit more than doubled year-on-year to ₹21,630 crore in the second quarter, supported by improved refining margins and a brief decline in benchmark crude oil prices.
Mr. Jain said LPG under-recoveries stood at ₹184 per cylinder in September before rising to ₹229 in October. These are projected to increase further to ₹309 in November and ₹370 in December.
Diversified crude basket
Explaining the volatility in procurement costs, he said crude purchases during the quarter ranged from a discount of $5 per barrel to a premium of $12 against prevailing benchmark prices. In the first quarter, the range was from zero discount or premium to a premium of $18 per barrel.
Effective procurement prices depend on several factors, including whether supplies are contracted on a free-on-board (FOB) or delivered-at-place (DAP) basis, freight costs and the grade of crude.
Russian crude accounted for around 55% of IOC’s crude basket during the first half of the fiscal, followed by supplies from the Middle East, primarily Saudi Arabia and Dubai, at 24%. Africa, including Angola and Nigeria, contributed about 10%, while Brazil accounted for 7%. Supplies from the U.S. and Venezuela made up the remaining 2-5% and 3-4%, respectively.
Around 87% of the company’s crude procurement during the period came through spot sourcing. Mr. Jain said.
Spot purchases not always expensive
Responding to a question on whether spot purchases entailed higher costs, he said such sourcing did not necessarily mean paying a premium, as prices varied across region/geography.
“Now, within spot you have Russian crude. Sometimes, we are getting a high discount, sometimes we are paying a premium as well,” Mr. Jain said.
“In the few months, we have seen huge, discounted crude coming in from Iraq. So, the moment it is available, we are buying huge quantities from Iraq also. That used to be our staple diet before the [West Asia] crisis as well.”
He added that procurement economics were also influenced by effective negotiations, which played an important role in determining the final price.

briefs.headline: GST Rules To Ease: Council clears simpler registration and faster refunds; small online sellers gain
briefs.deck: Starting November 1, new Goods and Services Tax procedures will offer a streamlined experience for businesses. Small online sellers can enjoy simplified registration and access to e-commerce operators' warehouses. The GST portal's enhanced user-friendliness will minimize registration errors. Automated refunds will speed up processing, reducing manual oversight. Additionally, businesses will have…
briefs.bodyText:
NEW DELHI: Starting November 1, businesses will see several changes in Goods and Services Tax (GST) procedures, with simpler registration, faster refunds and more flexible rules for discounts offered after a sale.
The changes, approved at the 57th GST Council meeting on October 8, are aimed at making GST compliance easier, particularly for small businesses and sellers operating through e-commerce platforms.
The reforms mainly cover GST registration, returns and refunds, along with the tax treatment of post-supply discounts. The Council's decisions requiring administrative changes will be implemented in phases beginning Sunday, November 1, 2026.
Easier GST registration for small online sellers
Small businesses selling products through e-commerce platforms across multiple states and Union Territories will no longer need to maintain a physical office in every state where their goods are stored.
Under the new rules, eligible sellers passing on input tax credit of up to Rs 2.5 lakh per month can use an e-commerce operator's warehouse as their principal place of business (PPoB) for GST registration in states where they do not have a physical presence.
However, sellers must have a genuine physical presence in at least one state, where Aadhaar authentication and physical verification will be carried out. For other states, they can obtain GST registration with the consent of the e-commerce platform, without further involvement of a tax officer.
The change is expected to benefit around 9.5 lakh small sellers, helping them expand their reach across India without the additional cost of setting up offices in multiple states. It is also expected to create greater tax parity between competing e-commerce business models.
GST registration to become simpler
Businesses applying for GST registration can also expect a smoother process from November 1.
The GST department has standardised the documents and information required for registration, making it easier for applicants to understand what they need to submit.
The GST portal will also offer a more user-friendly interface, with clearer navigation, drop-down lists and tooltips to guide applicants through the process.
These changes are expected to reduce errors, unnecessary queries and application rejections caused by missing or incorrect information, while speeding up registration approvals.
Faster GST refunds with automated approvals
Businesses waiting for GST refunds could receive their money faster under the new system, which reduces the need for manual intervention by tax officers.
Refund claims for the full excess balance available in a taxpayer's electronic cash ledger will be sanctioned automatically by the system, without requiring approval from a tax officer.
Similarly, for refund claims related to zero-rated supplies and an inverted duty structure, 90% of the claimed amount will be provisionally sanctioned through an automated process.
These provisional refunds will be based on the system's identification and assessment of risks, without direct intervention from tax officers.
The government is also easing GST rules for post-supply discounts, addressing a longstanding concern among businesses.
Under the revised framework, businesses will have greater flexibility to offer discounts after a sale without having to meet the earlier requirements of a pre-existing agreement or linking the discount to specific invoices.
However, safeguards related to credit notes and the corresponding reversal of input tax credit will remain in place.
The change is expected to benefit businesses that regularly offer volume-based incentives, trade schemes and year-end rebates.

briefs.headline: Textile industry welcomes customs duty exemption extension for cotton
briefs.bodyText:
With daily cotton arrivals remaining dull at fewer than 70,000 bales a day during the first month of the current cotton marketing season (October 2026 to September 2027) and the Government of India deciding to extend the customs duty exemption on cotton till the end of December, the textile industry hopes there will be adequate cotton to meet the rising demand.
The Confederation of Indian Textile Industry (CITI) chairman Ashwin Chandran said in a press release that the duty exemption would strengthen the international competitiveness of the Indian textile and apparel sector that is targeting $100 billion in exports by 2030.
Cotton imports do not displace domestic cotton. In May 2026, a joint study by Gherzi and the International Cotton Advisory Committee (ICAC) said Indian industry needs a cotton policy environment that will enable it to compete effectively with its Asian peers, which have duty-free access to international cotton.
Imports are necessary to bridge the demand-supply gap arising from reduced cotton production in India, he said.
“The extension of the cotton import duty waiver till December 31, 2026, will ensure that Indian textile and apparel companies can keep their input costs under control. The move will provide near-term predictability for the value chain, enabling companies to plan production cycles and honour export contracts better,” he said in a statement.
According to Durai Palaniswamy, chairman of the Southern India Mills Association, the industry is likely to have imported around 72 lakh bales during the 2025-2026 season taking advantage of temporary duty exemptions (from June 1 to October 31) and mitigating the domestic cotton shortage.
There was no import duty on cotton during 2008-2021 that ensured win-win strategy for both the cotton farmers and the industry. The Government levied import duty when the country was net exporter (30-70 lakh bales) of cotton and it gave temporary exemptions from 2022.
Mr. Palaniswamy said Indian cotton productivity is 430-440 kgs a hectare as against the world average of 815kgs/ha and over 1,500 kgs/ha productivity level being achieved by more than 20 countries.
Considering the urgent policy intervention for raw material security, he sought import duty exemption for all varieties of cotton till 2030.
